segments.text: Machine learning is worth reaching for
when a relationship is too tangled to
write down as rules, but examples of it
are sitting in your data.
Our running example is a fictional
retailer that wants to know, at the
moment a customer checks out, how long
the delivery will take and whether it
will arrive late. Those are supervised
problems. There is a target we
eventually observe, minutes to the door
or late versus on time, and we learn a
mapping from what we know at checkout to
that target. The same data also supports
unsupervised questions, where there is
no target at all, which customers behave
alike, how to compress many features
into a few, which orders look unusual.
But before any of that, write down the
baseline.
The carrier already publishes a promised
days table, and the median delivery time
per zone is one line of code. A model
has to beat that bar on the same
evaluation by enough to justify what it
costs to build and run. If the rule
already decides well, learning only adds
risk.
Every model in this course starts from a
contract, and it is worth writing down
before touching any data. The unit is
one order, not one customer and not one
day, so each row we learn from is an
order. The target for the first task is
the number of minutes from checkout to
the doorstep. For the second, an order
is late if it arrives after the promise
we showed at checkout, which means the
promise itself is fixed at that moment,
too.
The prediction time is the checkout
click, and that single point on the
order's timeline does a lot of work.
Anything that happens afterwards,
dispatch, the courier's route, the
actual delivery, simply does not exist
yet, so it cannot be a feature.
Finally, name the decision the
prediction changes, the promise
displayed to the customer, or whether to
offer an express upgrade. The contract
also states the claim. Do we mean future
orders, unseen customers, or both? Those
imply different splits, and the next
chapter depends on that answer.
Once the contract is fixed, every column
in the orders table gets exactly one
role. Features are what the model is
allowed to see, and the test is simple.
Was this value known at the checkout
click?
The delivery zone, the number of items
in the basket, the distance, and the
promise we displayed all pass. The
target is what we are learning to
predict. Duration in minutes for one
task and a late flag for the other.
Notice that late is derived from
duration and the promise, so it can
never also be a feature. Everything else
is metadata. The order ID, the customer
ID, the timestamp. Metadata is not junk
to discard.
The customer ID is how we will keep
whole customers out of training when the
claim is about new customers. The
timestamp is how we order rows in time
and enforce the cutoff. What metadata
must never become is a feature. And it
carries no general pattern. So, a model
that sees it can memorize individual
rows, and that looks like accuracy until
it meets an order it has never seen.
A label is only as good as the moment it
was taken. The curve on the left shows,
for orders of each age, what share has
actually been delivered. Look at 3 days.
About half of those orders are still in
transit. Their duration is not short. It
is unknown.
If we train on recent orders and keep
only the ones that have already arrived,
we quietly keep the fast deliveries and
drop the slow ones, and the model learns
that deliveries are quicker than they
really are.
The fix is a maturity window. Only
orders old enough that almost every
outcome is in. Here, 10 days count as
labeled. Some outcomes never arrive at
all.
A canceled order or a lost parcel has no
delivery time, so we either exclude it
and say so, or treat it as a separate
outcome with its own target. And even a
recorded label can be wrong. Delivery
times come from driver scans, which are
sometimes batched at the end of a route.
Check a sample against an independent
record before trusting the whole column.
Here are six rows from a raw extract,
and they already hide most of what can
go wrong. First, coverage. Nearly every
row is from the north zone. If that is
true of the whole extract, a model
trained on it supports a claim about the
north, not about every customer the
retailer serves.
Second, the first two rows are the same
order. A payment retry wrote it twice.
If one copy lands in training and the
other in evaluation, the model is graded
on an order it has already seen, so
duplicates come out before any split.
Third, customer C07 owns four of the six
rows.
Their orders share an address, a basket
style, and a courier route, so they are
not independent. If our claim is about
new customers, every order from a
customer has to sit on the same side of
the split. Fourth, the timestamps mix
UTC with a local offset.
For a claim about future orders, we sort
rows in time, and sorting is only
meaningful once every timestamp is in
one time zone.
Cleaning data is a series of decisions
about who the model is for, so each one
gets written down with a count. We start
from 120,000 raw orders. 1,800 are
payment retry duplicates.
300 have a delivery time earlier than
their checkout, which is not an unusual
order but a broken pipeline, and it is
worth finding out why. 9,400 are too
recent for their outcome to be known,
and 2,100 were canceled and have no
outcome at all.
That leaves 106,400
rows, and the claim we eventually make
covers only orders like those. Columns
get the same treatment with privacy in
mind. The model needs to know roughly
where an order is going, not the street
address, so the address becomes a
delivery zone.
The customer ID stays, but only as a
grouping key. Names, emails, and payment
details are never needed, so they are
never extracted. The less sensitive data
a data set carries, the less there is to
protect and the less there is to leak.
The last idea of this chapter is a
boundary on everything that follows. A
predictive model answers the question,
given how things currently work, what is
likely to happen to this order? It does
not answer what would happen if we
changed something. Here is how those get
confused. Under the old policy, the
express upgrade was offered mostly on
far orders, and far orders are late more
often. So, in the historical data,
express offered is a strong predictor of
lateness, and a model will happily use
it.
Read that as a cause, and you would
conclude that express makes deliveries
late and stop offering it. But, distance
drives both the offer and the lateness,
and the data cannot tell us what Express
itself does. Predictions are valid under
the policy that produced the data.
Estimating the effect of an action needs
a randomized experiment or causal
methods which belong to the probability
and statistics course. And once we act
on predictions, we change the data that
future models learn from which we come
back to in chapter 11.
